chapter_title: Learning Graphs, MicroSims, and Content Generation Rules
learning_objective: The learner will distinguish prerequisite graphs that contain a cycle from graphs that do not, in 6 small graphs, with at least 5 of 6 classified correctly.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** dag-cycle-spotter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/graph-algorithms/tree/main/docs/sims/dag-viewer
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish prerequisite graphs that contain a cycle from graphs that do not, in 6 small graphs, with at least 5 of 6 classified correctly. **Prerequisites:** concept dependency, edge direction, directed acyclic graph, cycle, topological order (all defined in the sections "Concept Dependency" and "Directed Acyclic Graph" above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each graph the learner commits to one label, "Valid (no cycle)" or "Has a cycle", before the sim reveals the answer. For a graph labeled "Has a cycle", the learner also selects the concepts that lie on the cycle. A graph is correct when the label matches the answer column and, for cycle graphs, the selected set equals the cycle set exactly. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Looking at the graph is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Two concepts that share a prerequisite form a cycle. (2) A graph with two disconnected parts is invalid. (3) A concept that depends on itself is not a cycle. (4) A longer chain of dependencies is more likely to contain a cycle. **Instructional Rationale:** Analyze-level distinguishing needs the learner to inspect structure and decide, so each graph is small enough to trace by eye but constructed so that surface features (a shared prerequisite, a long chain, two components) do not predict the answer. Committing a label before reveal turns tracing into evidence. **Content:** Each graph is a list of dependencies in the form "dependent needs prerequisite". Concepts are Fractions, Decimals, Percent, Ratios, Proportions, and Equations. The sim labels all graphs "synthetic example". | # | Dependencies | Answer | Cycle set | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Percent needs Decimals; Decimals needs Fractions; Ratios needs Fractions; Proportions needs Ratios | Valid (no cycle) | none | Every path ends at Fractions, which needs nothing, so a teaching order exists. | | 2 | Percent needs Decimals; Decimals needs Fractions; Fractions needs Percent | Has a cycle | Percent, Decimals, Fractions | Starting at Percent and following needs returns to Percent, so none of the three can be learned first. | | 3 | Equations needs Proportions; Equations needs Percent; Proportions needs Fractions; Percent needs Fractions | Valid (no cycle) | none | Two concepts sharing one prerequisite is normal; there is no path that returns to its start. | | 4 | Equations needs Proportions; Proportions needs Ratios; Ratios needs Equations; Ratios needs Fractions | Has a cycle | Equations, Proportions, Ratios | Equations, Proportions, and Ratios each need the next; the dependency on Fractions is fine but does not break the cycle. | | 5 | Decimals needs Fractions; Percent needs Ratios | Valid (no cycle) | none | Two separate chains are allowed; a graph does not have to be connected. | | 6 | Percent needs Percent; Percent needs Fractions | Has a cycle | Percent | A concept that needs itself is a cycle of length one, so it can never be learned first. | **Provenance:** The graphs are synthetic, constructed for this exercise, and the sim labels them "synthetic example". The definition of a cycle and a valid graph is the one stated in the chapter section "Directed Acyclic Graph". **Rules:** Graphs are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6, and each is a list of edges plus the set of concept names. A graph is "Has a cycle" if and only if some concept can reach itself by following needs, including by a single edge to itself. Disconnected graphs are valid. Each graph allows exactly one label commitment, and for cycle graphs one selection of cycle members, and both are final. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees graph 1 as a list of dependencies and its concept names. 2. The learner chooses "Valid (no cycle)" or "Has a cycle". 3. If the learner chose "Has a cycle", the sim asks them to select the concepts on the cycle, then the learner confirms. 4. The sim shows the correct label, the cycle set if there is one, and the Why text, and marks the graph correct or incorrect. 5. The learner repeats for graphs 2 to 6. The sim then shows the score and the misconception behind each missed graph. **Feedback:** Six graphs, fixed order, one committed answer each, and the answer is final. Correct: "Correct" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite" followed by the correct label, the cycle set, and the Why text. The correct answer is revealed immediately after the learner confirms. The final score reads "n of 6 correct". **Starting State:** Graph 1 is shown with no label chosen, and the question on screen is "Can these concepts be taught in some order?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that a learning graph must be a DAG, that a cycle makes teaching order impossible, that having several valid orders is normal, and that a graph may have shared prerequisites and disconnected parts.
